item.text: The continuation recovered material for every selected chapter. The strongest additions are technical nuclear-policy coverage, opened OHCHR/ICRC detention records, Russian-language domestic repression evidence, internet-control records, an independent retrospective of Istanbul negotiations, and documented—but still attribution-limited—Putin-linked asset evidence. I’m preserving later reports only where they directly document the 2022 period.

Review round 1 continuation completed. No scores or score ranges were assigned.

The sandbox remains read-only, so `research-materials.md` and `research-ledger-manifest.json` could not be updated physically. The following entries should be appended after `E018`; all are globally unique and preserve exact lens mappings.

## New evidence units

- **E019 — 1B:** Arms Control Association reports that the 27 February alert’s effects on nuclear forces and command-and-control were unclear; it also records Grom 2022 strategic nuclear exercises and notes that the invasion reduced prospects for post-New START arms-control progress. [Arms Control Association](https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2022-03/news/putin-orders-russian-nuclear-weapons-higher-alert), paragraphs covering command ambiguity, lines 92–109. Supports `1B.2`, `1B.3`, `1B.4`, `1B.7`, `1B.8`, `1B.10`. Final evidence, medium_high, technical NGO/arms-control source.

- **E020 — 1B/2B:** The same Arms Control Association report records February 2022 diplomatic openings, the US–Russia security proposals, Normandy-format meetings, and their failure before invasion. This provides both adverse and contrary/alternative-diplomacy context; it does not establish Putin’s personal negotiating intent. Locator: paragraphs 102–113. Supports `1B.4`, `1B.8`, `2B.1`, `2B.3`, `2B.7`, `2B.10`. Final evidence, medium_high.

- **E021 — 2B:** ICRC stated in October 2022 that it had visited hundreds but not thousands of POWs, and had been denied access to all POW locations, including Olenivka. It explains that access is required under the Third Geneva Convention. [ICRC](https://www.icrc.org/en/document/ukraine-russia-icrc-asks-immediate-and-unimpeded-access-to-all-prisoners-of-war), paragraphs 180–189. Supports `2B.4`, `2B.5`, `2B.9`. Final evidence, high, intergovernmental humanitarian monitor. This documents an access/accountability gap, not the treatment of every detainee.

- **E022 — 2B:** OHCHR’s March 2023 report, used retrospectively for the 2022 period, records 621 cases of enforced disappearance/arbitrary detention by Russian forces since 24 February 2022; 90% of interviewed released civilians reported torture or ill-treatment. It also records lack of Russian access for OHCHR and widespread mistreatment of Ukrainian POWs, including torture, executions and poor medical care. [OHCHR](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/UN-Human-Rights-Ukraine-released-reports-on-treatment-of-prisoners-of-war-and-overall-human-rights-situation-in-Ukraine), paragraphs 88–110. Supports `2B.4`, `2B.5`, `2B.9`, `2B.10`. Final evidence, high, retrospective but directly period-fit.

- **E023 — 2B:** OHCHR’s June 2022 report records credible reports of torture and ill-treatment of POWs in Russian custody and affiliated facilities, including Kursk, Taganrog and Olenivka; it also records closed confinement, lack of sanitation and lack of access. [OHCHR PDF](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3984286/files/2022-06-UkraineArmedAttack-EN.pdf), pp. 28–33, paragraphs 103–109. Supports `2B.4`, `2B.5`, `2B.9`. Final evidence, high. It also preserves contrary material concerning Ukrainian mistreatment, so it should not be represented as one-sided documentation.

- **E024 — 2B:** CSIS’s retrospective analysis of the April 2022 Istanbul Communiqué describes proposed neutrality, limits on military cooperation, unresolved territorial issues, conditional security guarantees and possible sanctions relief. [CSIS](https://www.csis.org/analysis/unfinished-plan-peace-ukraine-provision-provision), paragraphs 268–280. Supports `2B.1`, `2B.3`, `2B.7`, `2B.10`, `8B.1`, `8B.10`. Final evidence, medium_high, retrospective research analysis. It documents negotiation content, not why the talks failed or Putin’s personal decision at each stage.

- **E025 — 3B/4B/7B:** OVD-Info’s 2022 repression report documents police violence during spring and autumn protests, including beatings and strangulation; it records prosecutions of opposition figures, organizations declared extremist, religious prosecutions, anti-war criminal cases, and civil-society liquidations. [OVD-Info](https://ovd.info/en/repressions-russia-2022), paragraphs 74–75, 112–168, 198–227. Supports `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.5`, `3B.8`, `3B.9`, `4B.3`, `4B.6`, `4B.9`, `7B.6`, `7B.7`. Final evidence, medium_high, civil-society monitor. Attribution is to Russian authorities and law enforcement; it does not prove Putin personally ordered each incident.

- **E026 — 4B:** Freedom House’s Freedom on the Net 2022 report records Roskomnadzor’s blocking of Facebook, Twitter and Instagram, the Meta “extremist organization” case, and March 2022 orders moving state media away from foreign hosting and DNS. [Freedom House](https://freedomhouse.org/country/russia/freedom-net/2022), paragraphs 146–153. Supports `4B.3`, `4B.6`, `4B.9`, `4B.10`. Final evidence, medium_high.

- **E027 — 4B/3B:** Amnesty records the 24 February Roskomnadzor order requiring media to use only official sources and avoid “war,” “invasion” and “attack”; it also documents blocking of independent media and the departure of at least 150 journalists. [Amnesty International](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/03/russia-kremlins-ruthless-crackdown-stifles-independent-journalism-and-anti-war-movement/), paragraphs 67–78. Supports `3B.8`, `4B.3`, `4B.6`, `4B.9`. Final evidence, medium_high.

- **E028 — 3B:** Human Rights Watch documents anti-LGBT discrimination, failure to investigate threats, inadequate domestic-violence legislation and police response, forced returns of women from shelters, and poor treatment in institutions. [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2022/country-chapters/russia), paragraphs 181–200. Supports `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.4`, `3B.7`, `3B.10`. Final evidence, medium_high. Some claims concern systemic conditions or subnational actors; national ruler attribution remains limited.

- **E029 — 3B/4B:** The US State Department’s 2022 human-rights report lists credible reports of torture, prison abuses, arbitrary detention, minority violence, severe media/internet restrictions, political exclusion and lack of accountability for gender-based violence. [2022 Russia Human Rights Report](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089062.html), summary paragraph. Supports `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.4`, `3B.7`, `3B.8`, `4B.3`, `4B.6`, `4B.9`. Final evidence, medium_high, official human-rights reporting. The summary is broad; claim-specific chapter use should prefer underlying sections where available.

- **E030 — 7B:** OCCRP’s Russian Asset Tracker, updated through 4 August 2022, reports documentary tracing of assets linked to Putin’s circle and more than $19.8 billion in documented assets among Russian elites. [OCCRP](https://www.occrp.org/en/project/russian-asset-tracker), paragraphs 40–45. Supports `7B.3`, `7B.4`, `7B.6`, `7B.7`, `7B.9`, `7B.10`. Final evidence, medium_high, investigative consortium. This is evidence of networks and documentary tracing, not proof that Putin personally owned every listed asset.

- **E031 — 7B:** US Treasury identifies Sergei Roldugin as a close Putin associate and “custodian of President Putin’s offshore wealth,” and identifies yachts and entities in which Putin was assessed to have an interest. [US Treasury](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy0802), paragraphs 609–625 and 639–645. Supports `7B.3`, `7B.4`, `7B.6`, `7B.7`, `7B.9`. Final evidence, medium_high for the formal sanctions designation and official findings; attribution remains contested and should be labeled as a US government sanctions finding, not an adjudicated criminal judgment.

- **E032 — 5B/6B:** The IMF’s April 2022 analysis provides a favorable/mitigating policy record: Russian authorities used rate increases, foreign-exchange intervention, export-proceeds surrender, liquidity measures and social-benefit/wage spending to stabilize the economy after the invasion shock. This supplements E012 with the same report but distinct policy claims. [IMF PDF](https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Publications/REO/EUR/2022/April/English/text.ashx), p. 22, lines 1493–1508. Supports `5B.3`, `5B.9`, `6B.6`, `8B.6`, `8B.9`. Final evidence, high.

- **E033 — 5B/6B/8B:** The Russian government’s 2022 activity report claims almost 4 trillion rubles in transfers to regional budgets and support for infrastructure and social facilities, while acknowledging uneven regional conditions. [Russian Government](https://government.ru/news/48055/), 2022 government-report presentation. Supports `5B.6`, `5B.8`, `6B.2`, `6B.3`, `6B.9`, `8B.2`, `8B.6`. Context only, medium_low, official self-report; requires independent verification of implementation and distribution.

- **E034 — 8B:** The Russian government’s 2022 budget documentation provides a formal program/budget record for 2023 planning and the 2024–25 period. [Russian Government budget document](https://government.ru/docs/all/144850/). Supports `8B.1`, `8B.2`, `8B.6`. Context/final evidence only for the existence of formal budget decisions; it does not establish successful implementation or outcomes.

## Chapter continuation outcomes

- **1B:** Materially improved. Added independent arms-control analysis, command-and-control uncertainty, Grom 2022 exercise context, pre-invasion diplomatic alternatives and Belarus proliferation context. The central gap remains absence of independently verified internal command safeguards and a complete 2022 doctrine record. E006/E018 remain one IAEA family.
- **2B:** Materially improved. Added ICRC access failure, OHCHR POW/detention evidence, contrary Ukrainian-abuse evidence, and Istanbul negotiation content. Remaining gaps: Russian decision records, proxy/intelligence conduct, and causal attribution for negotiation failure.
- **3B:** Materially improved. Added domestic police brutality, torture reports, prison/systemic abuses, minority/LGBT and gender-based-violence material, and subnational attribution caveats. Direct evidence of effective remedies and positive corrective action remains sparse.
- **4B:** Materially improved. Added internet blocking, Roskomnadzor censorship orders, journalist exodus and broader repression records. Election-transfer evidence remains structurally limited because 2022 was not a federal presidential election year; regional and judicial-case evidence remains incomplete.
- **5B:** Slightly improved. Added formal government transfers and a clearer favorable stabilization record, but household distribution, realized inflation, budget execution, appointments and capture remain unresolved.
- **6B:** Slightly improved. The new social-spending and vulnerable-group evidence helps identify concrete themes, but there is still insufficient independent evidence on poverty, service delivery, housing, sanitation and social-protection outcomes.
- **7B:** Materially improved but still high attribution risk. OCCRP and Treasury provide personal-network and asset-tracing evidence, but both require careful distinction between documented network links, official sanctions findings and proven personal ownership/benefit. Direct statements, disclosures, corrections and appointment conflicts remain gaps.
- **8B:** Improved. Added formal budget/program records, regional transfers, stabilization measures and peace-negotiation implementation context. Independent evidence of a complete program portfolio, implementation quality, adaptation and durability remains incomplete.

## Rejected or limited candidates

- Wikipedia, Reddit reposts and search snippets remained discovery-only.
- ICRC access statements were not converted into claims that all POWs were mistreated.
- OHCHR’s 2023 material was retained only for facts explicitly referring to the period beginning 24 February 2022.
- Russian government budget and regional-transfer claims remain context or formal-record evidence, not independently verified outcomes.
- Treasury and OCCRP asset material was retained with attribution and contestation limits; it does not by itself establish a criminal finding or every claimed personal-benefit link.
- The Arms Control Association’s Grom and command-control material is technical context and does not establish a secret internal safeguard failure.

## Updated research gaps

The remaining highest-value gaps are:

1. A primary 2022 Russian nuclear doctrine or command-safeguard document.
2. Russian and Ukrainian negotiation records showing decision ownership and reasons for failure.
3. Direct domestic prison-monitoring and remedy evidence.
4. Household-level Russian poverty, inflation and regional welfare evidence.
5. Independent verification of asset ownership, appointments and personal-benefit mechanisms.
6. Audited implementation results for 2022 national programs and regional transfers.

No score, score range, anchor, ranking, or judge recommendation was produced.
